articles.author: Shiva Charan
articles.description:
This is the minimum YAML needed:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: my-container
      image: nginx:latest

apiVersion: v1


Pods always use API version v1.
kind: Pod


Defines the type of Kubernetes object.
metadata:


Name of your pod (must be unique in the namespace).
spec:


Describes what the Pod should run → containers.
containers:


A Pod must have at least one container.
2. Pod With Port, Environment Variables & Resource Limits







apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx-container
      image: nginx:latest
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      env:
        - name: ENVIRONMENT
          value: production
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: "256Mi"
          cpu: "500m"

3. Pod With Multiple Containers (Sidecar Pattern)







apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: multi-container-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app-container
      image: busybox
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo Hello from App; sleep 3600"]

    - name: log-container
      image: busybox
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo Logging; sleep 3600"]

Same Pod IP
Same network namespace
Volumes (if defined)
How to Create the Pod





Save the file as:
pod.yaml

Then apply:
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Check the pod:
kubectl get pods

Describe details:
kubectl describe pod my-pod

View logs:
kubectl logs my-pod

Define a YAML with
`apiVersion: v1`, 
`kind: Pod`,
metadata (name), and a 
spec with one or more containers. 

Then apply it using kubectl apply -f <file>
articles.title: 🧩 Basic Syntax for Creating a Pod

articles.author: Bhaskara teja Bulusu
articles.description:
How terraform updates Infrastructure ?


When we run the terraform apply command, some files are created such as terraform.tfstate, terraform.tfstate.backup and terraform compares desired state with the actual state and provision the resources and update the infrastructure accordingly.
Desired state: The infrastructure we wish to create
State file management
Storing the state files in the remote backend such as AWS S3 secures and stores separately which is easy to manage.
State file Best practices:
Store file to Remote backend
Don't update/delete the files
State locking --> a process which locks the file making the file inaccessible for others
Isolation of state file --> separate state files for different environments
Regular backup
Code for storing state files in the Remote backend (S3 Bucket)
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "bhaskaratejabulusu-state-files-day04"
    key = "dev/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-east-1"
    encrypt = true
    use_lockfile = true

  }
}

Make sure that the remote backend in this case S3 bucket is already created/available before running the terraform commands.
Security in S3 bucket:
S3 versioning enable
IAM minimal to S3
S3 Bucket Policy
Encryption (Server Side Encryption)
Access Logging
terraform state list




@piyushsachdeva
articles.title: Day-04: Terraform state file management using S3 Bucket
